Nothing is built. This is not in your planner and not in the copy planner. You asked me to park it — “don’t do anything on it yet… its just to remind me to do it later when this copy planner is done” — so this card is a reminder, nothing more.

I did measure the cause, so that when you do say go, the card starts from a fact rather than a guess. I ran your planner’s own describing code over thirteen kinds of change:

what you dowhat the Undo row says
change a task’s durationCall the accountant — duration 60 min → 90 min
rename a taskRenamed Call the accountant → Call the bookkeeper
delete or add a tasknames it
tick a task offdone empty → yes
move a taskChanged a task
rename an areaChanged a task
tally a habitChanged a task
write in the journalChanged a task
edit a noteChanged a task
add to a listChanged a task

Seven of thirteen come out useless — and the first of them is moving a task, which is probably what your four rows were, since they arrived within a minute of each other.

Why. Your planner already has a describer, and it is good at tasks — it was built in September for this same complaint. But it only ever looks at the task tree, while an Undo entry is recorded for every save. So a change anywhere else — areas, habits, the journal, notes, lists — has nothing to describe it and falls back to that one sentence. A move falls through too, because moving a task changes none of its fields, only its place.

What I would do when you say go: teach the existing describer the other five places and teach it about position, so a move reads “Moved Call the accountant under Work”. Not a second history — the one you have is fine, it just cannot see most of your planner.

You were right to separate these. Task history is yours. Restore is something I added to the same row, and describing both as one card made my addition look like part of your feature. This card is just the new button.

What it is. Your planner has been keeping backups since September — when you open it, every ten minutes while you work, before anything that replaces a lot at once, and when you close it. About twenty are kept. There has never been a way to see them. This is that way, and nothing more.

What it is not: a new backup system. It lists what is already being kept and calls the same code that already restores it. I built a second engine for this earlier and it broke the one you already had, so this one reuses rather than replaces.

your buildwith Restore
Past due(2)(2) — same

Deleted(1)(1) — same
Undo(6)(6) — same
Restore—(5) — the only addition

Measured with both builds driven for real, not read off the code: the four counts are identical, so your task history is provably untouched.

Restoring is safe to try. It MERGES rather than replaces, and it takes a fresh backup of right-now first — so pressing Restore can itself be undone. Driven in a browser: every seeded task survived, and clicking two different rows brought back the two different backups.
